How can you sell a house in Milwaukee when time matters?

Most Milwaukee owners choose between three routes: list with an agent, sell the house yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the property as it stands. The route that fits depends on the condition of the house, any open city orders, and how soon you need the money.

The Census Bureau estimated Milwaukee's population at 562,407 on July 1, 2025, down 2.7 percent from the April 2020 estimates base. Only 41.8 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, so a large share of Milwaukee houses that change hands are rentals, duplexes and investor-owned property. What kind of housing and neighborhoods does Milwaukee have?

Milwaukee sits on the western shore of Lake Michigan where the Milwaukee, Menomonee and Kinnickinnic rivers meet, and it is the seat of Milwaukee County. It was incorporated in 1846 and covers roughly 96 square miles of land, with about 6,001 people per square mile in 2020.

The housing stock reflects that history. The city is nicknamed Cream City for the pale local brick used on many older buildings, and its residential blocks include many Polish flats, two-family homes with one unit stacked above the other. An owner who lives upstairs and rents downstairs, or an heir who inherits a flat, often sells with tenants in place, so the lease terms matter to any buyer.

  • Revitalized areas named in the city's history include the Historic Third Ward, Lincoln Village, the East Side, Walker's Point and Bay View.
  • Bronzeville grew out of the Great Migration, and the South Side around Mitchell Street and Lincoln Village is tied to the city's Polish community.
  • Walker's Point takes its name from developer George H. Walker, who built a log house there in 1834.

What do schools, roads and jobs add to a Milwaukee listing?

Milwaukee Public Schools serves almost all of the city. It is the largest district in Wisconsin, with 69,115 students in 2021-2022 and 156 schools, and the city also has more than two dozen private or parochial high schools. Buyers with children will ask which attendance area or school option applies, so be ready to point them to the district.

Interstates 43 and 94 meet at the Marquette Interchange downtown, and Interstate 794 runs along the lakefront toward Bay View. Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport sits on the southern edge of the city, and The Hop streetcar links the Intermodal Station, downtown and the Lower East Side. Five Fortune 500 companies have headquarters here, and health care makes up about 27 percent of city jobs.

Weather is part of the sale too. Milwaukee averages about 48.7 inches of snow a year and 34.57 inches of precipitation, so buyers' inspectors look closely at roofs, gutters and basements.

What does the City of Milwaukee require when a house is sold?

The Department of Neighborhood Services (DNS) runs the main local checks. Its Title Search page strongly urges a DNS title search on every Milwaukee real estate transaction, because the form shows pending code violations, special charges and city programs that govern the property. The page states that the new owner is responsible for any unabated code violations.

  • Property registration: non-owner-occupied residential property and commercial property must be registered with DNS. Owner-occupied one-family, two-family and condo units are generally exempt. A seller uses the Seller Notification Form (DNS-8D) to tell DNS that ownership changed. Call (414) 286-8569 with questions.
  • Vacant building registration: a building left vacant for 30 days or more must be registered. A buyer of a vacant building registers within 30 days, and the seller must tell the buyer in plain terms that the registration is required. Listing the building for sale does not remove the duty.
  • Estates: a vacant property in probate is exempt when the personal representative or executor lives within the seven-county area around Milwaukee.
  • Open orders: DNS posts violations in its Land Management System, and you can call the section that issued an order.

The vacant building rules are in the city's Vacant Building FAQs. There is no fee for the first six months of registration, and renewals after that carry fees that DNS lists.

Which Wisconsin rules apply to a Milwaukee sale?

Sellers of one-to-four unit homes must complete a real estate condition report under Wis. Stat. 709.02. The buyer must receive it within 10 days after the seller accepts the contract, and a buyer who does not may rescind within two business days after those 10 days end. A court-appointed fiduciary who never lived in the house is excused, which matters for estate sales.

Under Wis. Stat. 77.22 the grantor pays a transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value. On a $200,000 sale that works out to $600. Transfers by will, or between a parent and child for nominal consideration, are among the exemptions listed in section 77.25. The return is filed electronically with the Department of Revenue, and the register of deeds collects the fee at recording.

How do you record the deed in Milwaukee County?

The Milwaukee County Register of Deeds is at 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103. Recording costs $30 per document no matter the page count, plus the transfer fee shown on your e-RETR receipt. The office takes cash, check or money order, and it does not take credit or debit cards.

  1. Prepare the deed with an attorney or title company, because the register cannot draft or review documents.
  2. File the electronic transfer return with the Department of Revenue and print the receipt.
  3. Submit the original deed, receipt and payment in person or by mail.

Documents are recorded in order of receipt within three to five business days, and the original is mailed back within one to two weeks. Questions go to (414) 278-4005.

How do assessments and tax bills affect a Milwaukee seller?

The Milwaukee Assessor's Office typically revalues the whole city every year and did so for 2026. Open Book for 2026 ran from April 20 to May 18, 2026, and that window has closed, so check the assessor's page for the next schedule. You can look up any property's assessed value at assessments.milwaukee.gov, and the assessor's phone line is (414) 286-6565.

The Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners explains that assessments reflect market value as of January 1. Clerks mail bills by the third Monday in December. If you pay in installments, the first is due January 31 and the second July 31, and an unpaid first installment becomes fully delinquent on February 1 with interest at 1 percent a month. Ask your title company how the current year's tax will be divided between you and the buyer at closing.

What if the Milwaukee house is a short-term rental or has tenants?

DNS administers the state tourist rooming house license for stays shorter than one month, and an owner who is ending that use submits a surrender form. Tenants and registration status are the usual issues in a rental sale, so gather leases, rent rolls and DNS registration records before you speak with buyers.

A cash buyer can purchase a tenant-occupied duplex or a house with open orders as it stands. Whichever route you take, ask for the offer in writing and compare the net amount after your mortgage payoff, city charges and closing costs.

Frequently asked questions

Does Milwaukee require a title search before I sell?

The city strongly urges one on every transaction but its page does not call it a legal requirement. The DNS title search shows open violations, special charges and registration duties, so it protects both sides.

Who pays the Wisconsin real estate transfer fee?

The seller, who is the grantor, pays it under Wis. Stat. 77.22 at 30 cents per $100 of value. The register of deeds collects it when the deed is recorded, and exempt transfers such as those by will owe nothing.

Do I have to register a vacant Milwaukee house I am selling?

Yes, if the building has been vacant 30 days or more and no exemption applies. Listing it for sale does not excuse the duty, and the buyer must register within 30 days of buying.

How long does recording a deed take in Milwaukee County?

The register records documents within three to five business days, in the order received. Paper originals come back by mail within one to two weeks.

Must I give the buyer a condition report?

Yes for most one-to-four unit homes. The report is due within 10 days after the contract is accepted, and a fiduciary who never occupied the home is exempt under Wis. Stat. 709.01.

What should a seller know about Madison itself?

Madison is the state capital, in the middle of Dane County, 77 miles west of Milwaukee and 122 miles northwest of Chicago. Downtown sits on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona, and the city wraps around the separate municipalities of Maple Bluff, Monona and Shorewood Hills. It also borders Sun Prairie, Middleton, McFarland and Fitchburg. On October 31, 2022, Madison annexed most of the remaining Town of Madison, so confirm the municipality printed on your tax bill before assuming which rules apply.

More than 120 neighborhood associations are officially recognized. The Marquette neighborhood on the near east side includes the Marquette Bungalows Historic District and the Orton Park Historic District, and Dudgeon-Monroe near Lake Wingra and the Hilldale area are other named areas buyers search by. Ask the city whether a historic district covers your block.

Jobs come from the state government, UW-Madison (more than 25,000 faculty and staff), UW Health, Meriter, St. Mary's, and employers such as Exact Sciences and Promega. The Madison Metropolitan School District serves the city with about 25,000 students in 46 schools, including Vel Phillips Memorial, Madison West, Madison East and La Follette high schools. What if the Madison house has been a short-term rental?

The permit does not pass to the buyer. Madison issues a ZTRHP permit to a specific host for a specific dwelling unit, and the permit is not transferable. The city calls these rentals short-term when guests stay fewer than 30 nights, and Wisconsin law calls them tourist rooming houses. If you advertised the house on Airbnb or VRBO, close out the listings and tell the buyer the permit ends with you.

These are the rules the city lists for permit holders:

  • The unit must be the host's primary dwelling while the rental runs and for the 12 consecutive months before it began.
  • When the host is away, the rental may operate no more than 30 days per licensing year, which runs July 1 to June 30.
  • Maximum guests are the lesser of twice the number of legal bedrooms or 12 people, and children under 12 do not count.
  • The permit costs a $300 one-time application fee and $100 a year to renew.
  • Violations carry fines of $500 to $1,000 per day, and the city can revoke the permit.

A Transient Room Tax permit from the city Finance Department and a license from Public Health Madison and Dane County are also required, and the city will not issue the ZTRHP permit until both are in hand. Ask Building Inspection to confirm your permit status in writing before you list the house.

How do rentals and tenants affect a Madison sale?

Tenants stay in place while you sell, so the buyer inherits the lease and the maintenance history. Madison Building Inspection takes complaints from tenants when a housing provider is slow to repair problems, and a complaint on file can surface in a buyer's questions. Fix open items first and keep repair receipts together.

Check the lease for its end date and any notice terms before you promise a closing date. If you want the unit vacant at closing, plan the timeline around the lease and the state landlord-tenant rules published by the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, which the city links as a resource for owners.

How does the Madison assessment calendar work?

The assessor values property as of January 1, and the objection steps run in spring and summer. For 2026, notices were mailed May 1, the Open Book window ran May 4 to 8, and objections to the Board of Assessors were due by 4:30 p.m. on May 15. Those 2026 dates have passed, so a 2027 appeal would follow the dates the Assessor's Office posts next spring.

Open Book is for correcting facts such as room counts or a permit that was not finished by January 1. If the facts are right but the value is not, you file an objection with the Board of Assessors, and the Board of Review is the final municipal step. Call 608-266-4531 or email openbook@cityofmadison.com. Commercial and multi-unit owners must include income and expense information with an objection.

What does Wisconsin require from a Madison seller?

Two state rules apply to almost every sale. The seller pays a transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value, set by Wis. Stat. 77.22, and the seller of a one-to-four unit property must furnish a condition report under Wis. Stat. 709.02. At the Madison median home value of $372,900, the fee works out to about $1,119.

  • The condition report is due within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A buyer who does not receive it can rescind within 2 business days after that 10-day period.
  • Court-appointed fiduciaries who never lived in the property are excused from the report.
  • Transfers by will or descent, foreclosure deeds to the lender and transfers between spouses are among the fee exemptions listed by the Department of Revenue.
  • A false or understated value on the return can bring a penalty of $25 or 25% of the extra fee, whichever is greater.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is still receives the report, and the return is still filed.

How is the deed recorded in Dane County?

The Dane County Register of Deeds records the deed for a $30 fee per document, and an Electronic Transfer Return receipt must accompany it. The deed must name the grantor and grantee, carry the grantor's notarized signature, include the legal description and the parcel number from the tax bill, and list a return address. Only the original deed with original signatures can be recorded, not a photocopy.

You can mail the package to the Dane County Register of Deeds, PO Box 1438, Madison, WI 53701-1438, with the recording fee and any transfer fee combined on one check. The office takes questions at (608) 266-4141. Deeds are usually drafted by an attorney or title company, and the office cannot fill them out for you.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit to rent my Madison house short term?

Yes. Madison requires a ZTRHP permit before you advertise or rent, and the house must be your primary dwelling. You also need a Transient Room Tax permit and a Public Health license. The city charges a $300 application fee and $100 a year to renew.

Does a short-term rental permit transfer to the buyer of my Madison house?

No. The city issues the permit to a specific host for a specific unit, and it cannot be transferred. A buyer who wants to operate a short-term rental must apply on their own and meet the primary-dwelling rule.

Who pays the Wisconsin transfer fee when I sell in Madison?

The seller pays it. Wis. Stat. 77.22 sets the fee at 30 cents per $100 of value, collected when the deed is recorded. Some transfers, such as those by will or between spouses, are exempt.

How long does the Madison buyer have to receive the condition report?

Ten days after the contract is accepted. If the report does not arrive in that time, the buyer has 2 business days after the 10-day period ends to rescind and recover deposits under Wis. Stat. 709.02.

Where do I record a deed for a Madison house?

File it with the Dane County Register of Deeds. The recording fee is $30 per document, and you must include the Electronic Transfer Return receipt. The mailing address is PO Box 1438, Madison, WI 53701-1438.

Jean Nicolet is believed to have landed near the site in 1634, and a French fur-trading post followed. Charles Michel de Langlade, who is generally credited as the first permanent European settler in Wisconsin, settled in Green Bay in the 1760s. The Tank Cottage, built in 1776, is the oldest standing building from the state's early years and now sits at Heritage Hill State Historical Park in neighboring Allouez.

That long history shows up in the housing stock. Winters are the main wear on a house: the January mean temperature is 16.6 degrees, and 68 days a year stay at or below freezing. Which Green Bay projects need a permit, and what if I skipped one?

Green Bay requires a building permit for most projects other than cosmetic ones, and the city's permit guide lists what counts. Work done without a permit can come up when a buyer or lender reviews the house, so check your own records first.

An owner who lives in the house may pull permits and do the work. Fences over 50 feet and sheds over 50 square feet need permits, while smaller ones do not, although zoning setbacks still apply. The initial application costs $500 and a renewal costs $250. A permit runs from July 1 through June 30, and renewals open on April 1. Missing the June 30 deadline voids the permit. Applicants submit proof of registration for Brown County room tax, a Brown County Health Department inspection report, proof of insurance and a local representative who is within 30 minutes of the property. The city says review can take up to 14 business days.

If you are selling a house that has run as a rental, tell your buyer which of those steps are current. A buyer who plans to continue the rental should budget the fee and the timeline.

The report is a disclosure and not a warranty. If you are a court-appointed fiduciary who never lived in the house, you are excused. No. The permit is non-transferable when the property is sold, so the buyer has to apply for a new one and pay the $500 initial fee.

Kenosha sits on Lake Michigan in southeastern Wisconsin, about 32 miles south of Milwaukee and 49 miles north of Chicago, with the Metra Union Pacific North line ending at its station. It was settled in 1835 as Pike Creek, renamed Southport in 1837, and took the Kenosha name when it became a city in 1850.

For most of the 20th century the city built cars. Rambler, Nash, Hudson and American Motors vehicles came off Kenosha lines until 1988, and the former AMC lakefront plant site became HarborPark, now lakeside condominiums, a marina and the Kenosha Public Museum. Today Snap-on and Jockey International have their headquarters here, and outlying business parks hold warehouses and distribution centers.

Locals describe three areas:

  • Downtown and HarborPark: the lakefront, with Allendale directly to the south.
  • Uptown: a mixed residential and small-business area that includes Brass, Lincoln Park and Wilson Heights.
  • West of the I: the part of the city beyond Interstate 94, which residents often call "the county."

Buyer interest differs by area, so a seller in Wilson Heights and one in HarborPark should expect different comparable sales and different buyer pools.

Why do commuting, schools and winters matter to Kenosha buyers?

They set who shops for your house and what they look for. Nearly half of the city's workforce commutes outside Kenosha County, and a 2016 study found many of those workers hold jobs in healthcare, manufacturing and professional services. Lower housing costs than the Chicago area draw them, so a house close to I-94 or the Metra station tends to appeal to that group.

Families look at Kenosha Unified School District, which runs 23 public elementary schools, five middle schools, seven charter schools and six high schools, among them Bradford, Tremper, Indian Trail and Reuther Central. Students also live near the University of Wisconsin-Parkside, Carthage College and the Gateway Technical College campus.

Weather shapes inspections. NOAA normals show about 37.6 inches of precipitation and 36.2 inches of snow in a typical year, the record low is minus 31 degrees Fahrenheit, and the city has had blizzards that dropped 19 and 23 inches. Buyers' inspectors in a climate like that spend time on roofs, gutters, basements and furnaces, so those are the items most likely to appear in a repair request. A cash buyer prices them in and skips the negotiation.

What are the steps and costs when a Kenosha house changes hands?

Wisconsin charges the seller, not the buyer, a transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction thereof (Wis. Stat. 77.22). On a $225,000 sale that works out to $675. The Kenosha County Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded, and the county keeps 20 percent while the balance goes to the state.

The steps run in this order:

  • Sign the purchase contract and open title work.
  • Complete the electronic Real Estate Transfer Return on the Wisconsin Department of Revenue site. The county requires the eRETR receipt for every conveyance that is not exempt.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds, 1010 56th Street, Kenosha. Real estate documents are recorded Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. A satellite office operates at 19600 75th Street in Bristol.
  • Pay off any mortgage, lien or unpaid tax from the proceeds.

Transfers by will, descent or survivorship are exempt from the fee under Wis. Stat. 77.25, as are transfers from a parent to a child for nominal consideration. An heir who later sells an inherited Kenosha house still pays the fee on that sale, because the sale itself is not exempt.

Do Kenosha sellers have to give the buyer a condition report?

Usually yes. Chapter 709 of the Wisconsin Statutes requires an owner who sells a property with one to four dwelling units to give the buyer a completed Real Estate Condition Report within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A buyer who does not receive it may rescind within two business days after those 10 days end and get the deposit back (Wis. Stat. 709.02).

Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-appointed fiduciaries who have never lived in the house are excused from the report, which matters for estates. Transfers that are exempt from the transfer fee are also exempt from the report. Ask the closing attorney or title company whether your sale falls under an exemption.

How are Kenosha property taxes handled at closing?

The tax bill for the year is divided between you and the buyer at closing, and any unpaid balance is paid from your proceeds. Wisconsin lets owners pay real estate tax in two equal installments, due January 31 and July 31, and a bill under $100 is due in full by January 31 (Wis. Stat. 74.11). If a first installment is not received within five working days after January 31, the entire unpaid balance becomes delinquent, and interest and penalties run from the preceding February 1.

The transfer itself by will or descent carries no Wisconsin transfer fee, so the heir does not owe it for inheriting. The later sale to a buyer is a new conveyance with the 30 cent fee. Ask a tax professional about income tax on any gain.

Wisconsin real estate tax is due in two installments, January 31 and July 31, unless the bill is under $100 or the municipality has adopted a multi-installment ordinance. A late payment can make the full remaining balance delinquent, so settle it before listing.

What should a Waukesha seller know about the city?

Waukesha is an older, fully built city with a long record as a spa town. Settlers arrived in 1834, the community took the name Waukesha in 1847, it became a village in 1852 and was chartered as a city in 1896. Mineral springs earned it the nicknames Spring City and Saratoga of the West.

The Census Bureau lists 25.52 square miles of land and 2,788.1 residents per square mile in 2020. Several features shape how buyers see a Waukesha address:

  • Water supply. The city switched from groundwater with radium above federal limits to Lake Michigan water in 2023, with the supply and return pipelines finished in 2024. Typical city water bills were projected to rise about 50 percent between 2023 and 2027, so expect buyers to ask about utility costs.
  • Schools. The Waukesha School District serves the city with three high schools (Waukesha North, South and West), four middle schools and 12 elementary schools. Catholic Memorial High School is a private option.
  • Colleges. Carroll University opened in 1846 and Waukesha County Technical College has a downtown campus. The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee at Waukesha operated from 1966 to 2025.
  • Getting around. Waukesha Metro Transit runs fixed routes and dial-a-ride service inside the city, and Badger Bus, Flixbus, Lamers and Wisconsin Coach Lines provide intercity service.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 put the median value of an owner-occupied home in Waukesha at $315,500 and the owner-occupied housing rate at 58.8 percent. Median gross rent is $1,219. The city has 30,567 households, an average of 2.27 people each, and a median household income of $83,837 in 2024 dollars.

What does Wisconsin law require when I sell my Waukesha house?

Wisconsin requires the owner of a one-to-four unit residential property to give the buyer a completed real estate condition report, and a buyer who misses that deadline may cancel. Under Wis. If it does not arrive, the buyer has two business days after those 10 days to rescind and get deposits back.

Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-supervised fiduciaries who have never lived in the property are excused from the report. So are transfers that are exempt from the transfer fee. If you inherited a Waukesha house and never occupied it, ask the probate attorney or title company whether the exemption applies to you.

The grantor also owes the state real estate transfer fee. Section 77.22 sets it at 30 cents for each $100 of value, which works out to $3 per $1,000. The register collects it when the deed is recorded, and the return must be filed electronically and signed by both grantor and grantee. Section 77.24 splits the money, with 20 percent staying with the county and the rest going to the state.

Waukesha property tax bills come from the city clerk and treasurer, and the city collects from mid-December through July 31 before records pass to the Waukesha County Treasurer. The city's tax page lists a full payment or first installment due January 31, then installments on March 31 and May 31. The two to watch are building permits and property maintenance. Waukesha requires inspections for new construction, alterations and repairs, for electrical, plumbing and HVAC work, and for changes in occupancy. Work done without a permit can surface when a buyer's inspector asks about it, so gather your permit history early.

Property maintenance falls under Chapter 17 of the city code, which says the owner must keep the structure and exterior in the condition the chapter requires and may not allow occupancy of premises that are unsafe or unsanitary. Inspectors can be reached Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the city site has forms for reporting tall grass and other complaints. The Waukesha County Register of Deeds records the deed, charges $30 for a standard document and accepts payment by check or money order only. Any transfer fee shown on your transfer return receipt is added to the same payment. Recording questions go to 262-548-7585 or recording@waukeshacounty.gov, and the office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays.

The office does not supply blank deeds or legal advice. A title company or real estate attorney normally prepares the deed and files the electronic return. You pay the City of Waukesha Clerk/Treasurer from mid-December through July 31. After July 31 the records move to the Waukesha County Treasurer, who collects delinquent real estate taxes. The city lets you pay online, by mail, at Waukesha State Bank, in a drop box or at City Hall.

The deed goes to the Winnebago County Register of Deeds, which explains that the deed must carry the grantor's notarized signature, a legal description, a return address and the parcel number from the tax bill. The city began in 1845, when commissioners chose a westward bend in the Milwaukee River for a settlement because the river could power mills. West Bend became a village in 1868 and a city in 1885, and it annexed the Village of Barton on November 1, 1961. Between 1950 and 1990 the population grew from 6,849 to 23,916 as US 45 made it practical to live in West Bend and work elsewhere. A house built in that postwar growth is now several decades old, which is why buyers look hard at the roof, furnace and basement.

The local economy grew from manufacturing and financial services; West Bend Mutual Insurance was founded in the city in 1894. Many residents now work in neighboring communities. Sign up for the Washington County LandNotification alert, which emails you when a document is recorded under your name or parcel. The Census Bureau's figures describe a high-value, owner-occupied market. What is Muskego like, and how did the city develop?

Muskego is a city in Waukesha County and part of the Milwaukee metropolitan area. Its name comes from a Potawatomi word meaning sunfish. The first European arrived in 1827, the Potawatomi ceded their Wisconsin lands in 1833, and the Luther Parker family from New Hampshire became the first permanent settlers. A largely agricultural area for generations, Muskego was incorporated as a city in 1964 and has grown through new housing developments into a bedroom community for Milwaukee. It also has a large Norwegian American population.

The city has about 36 square miles in total, of which 4.38 square miles is water. Density is low, at roughly 792 people per square mile in 2020, and 20.7 percent of residents are 65 or older. The Tess Corners Fire Department, a volunteer department, serves the city.

How do Muskego's lakes affect a home sale?

Three lakes lie inside city limits, and the lake a house faces shapes the questions buyers ask. Big Muskego Lake covers about 2,260 acres in the south-central part of the city and is shallow, with cattail marsh along its edges. Little Muskego Lake is 506 acres, reaches 65 feet at its deepest, and most of its shoreline is developed with houses. Lake Denoon covers 162 acres in the southwest.

  • Waterfront buyers ask about shoreline rules, so gather your survey, any pier or retaining-wall records and permits.
  • Big Muskego Lake is mostly under four feet deep with a muck bottom, while Little Muskego Lake averages 14 feet, so describe the lake your house sits on accurately.
  • Little Muskego Lake hosts boating, skiing, sailing and fishing, which many waterfront buyers want to hear about.

For questions about work near the water, call the Building Inspection Division at (262) 679-4145 before you promise a buyer anything about what can be built or changed.

Which schools serve Muskego houses?

The Muskego-Norway School District serves the city. Its schools include Bay Lane, Lakeview (which serves Muskego residents but sits in the Town of Norway) and Mill Valley elementary schools, Muskego Lakes Middle School and Lake Denoon Middle School, and Muskego High School. Two parochial options are St. Leonard K-8 Catholic School and St. Paul's Evangelical Lutheran Grade School.

That list gives you something concrete to put in a listing. A buyer comparing houses will ask which elementary school covers the address, and the district can answer by street.

What do Muskego's short-term rental rules mean for a seller?

If your Muskego house has been rented to guests, check Chapter 297 of the city code. Operating a short-term rental more than 10 nights in a license year requires a city license from the City Clerk, plus a Wisconsin tourist rooming house license and a seller's permit from the Department of Revenue unless exempt. The council adopted the chapter on April 12, 2022.

  • Each license runs January 1 through December 31 and is renewed yearly.
  • The owner must carry liability insurance and be reachable from 8:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. on rental days.
  • Guests must sign a register, and a unit cannot be rented to more than one party within a six-day period.
  • Violations bring forfeitures of $200 to $1,000 for each offense, and each day counts separately.

A buyer who plans to keep renting should ask the City Clerk about applying for a license in their own name. Clear any unpaid city charges first, since the chapter bars issuing or renewing a license with money owed to the city.

What permits and inspections should you know about in Muskego?

The Building and Inspection Services Division is at W182 S8200 Racine Ave. Inspections run Monday to Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and office hours are Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 8:00 to 9:00 a.m. Call (262) 679-4037 to schedule an inspection or ask a technical question, and (262) 679-4145 for general questions about the permit process. The division's Building Inspection page links to code, fee and permit information.

When a finished basement, deck or addition has no closed permit, call before you list. A buyer's inspector may ask for permit records, and settling the file early keeps a contract on schedule.

Which Wisconsin sale rules apply in Muskego?

The condition report rule in Wis. Stat. 709.02 covers houses with one to four units. A completed report must reach the buyer within 10 days of acceptance, or the buyer can cancel in the next two business days and recover deposits. Section 709.02 also lets a seller rely on written findings from an engineer, surveyor, pest control operator or contractor for matching entries.

The transfer fee under Wis. Stat. 77.22 is 30 cents per $100 of value, paid by the grantor. At the $417,400 median home value in Muskego, that fee is $1,252.20 (4,174 hundreds at 30 cents).

How do you record a deed with the Waukesha County Register of Deeds?

Muskego lies in Waukesha County. The Recording page lists $30 for standard documents such as deeds and mortgages. The office accepts check or money order made out to the Register of Deeds only, with no cash, credit or debit. If a transfer fee is due, include it with the payment.

Provide an email address or a self-addressed stamped envelope so the recorded document can come back. Email returns are immediate, and mailed returns take two to three weeks. The office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays at 262-548-7585 and cannot give legal advice, so use a title company or attorney for the deed itself.

When are Muskego property taxes due?

The Wisconsin Department of Revenue's Guide for Property Owners explains that first-half payments are due January 31 and second-half payments July 31. Late first installments make the whole balance delinquent on February 1. Ask the City of Muskego treasurer for the current bill and any special charges before your closing, and let the closing agent divide the year's tax.

Assessments follow market value on January 1, and owners who disagree can use the Open Book and Board of Review process described in the guide. Ask the city assessor for this year's dates.

When is a cash sale the better fit in Muskego?

A cash buyer fits a Muskego seller who wants fewer steps: no showings, no buyer loan to approve, and no repair list negotiated after an inspection. A listing can bring a higher price from a buyer who finances, and you give up some speed.

Do I need a license to rent my Muskego house short term?

Yes, for more than 10 nights in a license year. Chapter 297 requires a city license from the City Clerk, a Wisconsin tourist rooming house license and, unless exempt, a Department of Revenue seller's permit.

Who inspects buildings in Muskego?

The city's Building and Inspection Services Division does. Call (262) 679-4037 to schedule an inspection or (262) 679-4145 for general permit questions.

What lakes are in Muskego?

Big Muskego Lake, Little Muskego Lake and Lake Denoon lie within city limits. They cover about 2,260, 506 and 162 acres respectively.

Can the Waukesha County Register of Deeds take a credit card?

No. The office accepts check or money order made payable to the Register of Deeds for recording fees.

What does selling a house in De Pere, WI involve?

De Pere is a city in Brown County, about five miles south of Green Bay on the Fox River, with a 2025 Census Bureau estimate of 25,590 residents. A sale here runs through three local offices: the City of De Pere for permits and assessment, the Brown County Register of Deeds for the deed, and the Brown County Treasurer for tax records.

You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house as it stands. The sections below cover the De Pere details that affect price and timing under each route.

What is De Pere like, and how does the layout affect a home sale?

De Pere grew up around the first and last rapids on the lower Fox River. A French Jesuit mission was founded there in 1671, and the city traces its modern plat to 1836, when the De Pere Hydraulic Company laid out the town. The east and west banks were separate municipalities for decades. East De Pere became a city in 1883, and West De Pere (briefly named Nicolet) was folded into it in 1890, according to the city's Wikipedia entry.

That two-bank history still shapes the market. Large older homes line Broadway, Ridgeway Boulevard, Morris, Fulton, Franklin and nearby streets close to the river, and several of those blocks sit in National Register historic districts. St. Norbert College, founded in 1898, borders the river on the west side. Newer subdivisions sit away from the water, with Interstate 41 running along the west side of the city and Highways 32 and 57 entering from the south.

The city says two school districts serve De Pere, so check which one covers your address before you tell a buyer. Wikipedia also notes that the Lower Fox River below the De Pere dam went through a cleanup of PCB-contaminated sediment that was completed in 2020. If you are selling a riverfront house, buyers are likely to ask about it, so it helps to have the answer ready.

How does De Pere assess property, and what can you do about it?

Since 2018 De Pere has reassessed every property each year, so the city's values stay close to market. The city contracts the work to Accurate Appraisal, LLC of Menasha, and its assessment page explains that an assessor does not set tax rates and that a revaluation does not raise the total tax the city collects. The city's own explainer reported an overall average increase of about 8 to 10 percent in the 2024 update.

  • Open Book is a short conference, in person or by phone, with an assessor to review your value.
  • If you still disagree, you can appeal to the Board of Review, a five-member board of residents appointed by the mayor.
  • You schedule that appearance through the City Clerk at 339-4050 and file a Formal Objection Application. State law treats the assessor's value as correct until you prove otherwise with facts.

The city tells owners to call the Brown County Treasurer at (920) 448-4074 when the mailing address for a property changes, so tax bills reach the right person. After a sale, give the treasurer the buyer's mailing address so the next bill goes to the right place, and ask the title company how the current year's tax is split at closing.

Which De Pere permit rules matter before you sell?

The city's Building Inspection page tells buyers they can request city building records to see whether permits were obtained and whether work passed inspection. That makes permit history a negotiation point. Before listing, ask the Building Department (920-339-4053, dpbldg@deperewi.gov) for the record on your parcel.

  • A permit is required for new construction, repairs, additions, alterations and demolitions, including boilers, furnaces, wiring, plumbing fixtures, garages, porches, fences, decks, swimming pools and sheds.
  • Starting work without a permit doubles the permit fee, and a stop work order can follow.
  • A building permit lasts one year, or two years for a one- or two-family dwelling.
  • Replacing windows or changing exits and light openings can also need a permit.

The city warns that projects not completed to code can affect a home's insurability and potential sale. If you find open work, finishing and closing the permit before you list often settles the question for a buyer. If you cannot meet zoning or code requirements, the Zoning Board of Appeals hears variance requests for a $175 fee.

Can you rent out a De Pere house before selling it?

Long-term tenants are common in De Pere, and the city also regulates short-term rentals. Anyone who rents a house on a platform like Airbnb or VRBO needs a Tourist Rooming House license, which in De Pere is a two-step process. You first apply to the Development Services Department with a $100 fee, and after approval the Health Department's sanitarian explains how to get the license. The city says you may not rent the property until the sanitarian completes a pre-inspection.

If your house has been used as a short-term rental, ask the city's Development Services Department about its license status before you list. A buyer who plans to continue the use will ask.

De Pere deeds are recorded at the Brown County Register of Deeds, Northern Building Room 260, 305 E. Walnut Street, Green Bay. The office is open Monday to Thursday 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. and Friday 7:30 to 11:30 a.m., and walk-in real estate recordings are accepted until 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and until 10:30 a.m. on Friday. The phone number is 920-448-4470.

Brown County has moved to tag-less recording. If you submit paper documents, you also submit a Swift Agreement, and you receive an email with a secure link that allows up to three printed copies for seven days.

The deed also needs the state transfer return. Wis. Stat. 77.22 sets the fee at 30 cents per $100 of value, paid by the grantor, and requires the return to be filed electronically. The register writes the fee on the face of the deed, and if a sale is exempt, the exemption reason must be stated on the deed.

What must a De Pere seller disclose to the buyer?

Chapter 709 applies to sales, exchanges and land contracts of property with one to four dwelling units, and to vacant land. The chapter's definition excludes dwellings that have never been inhabited. The owner completes the state's condition report and delivers it within 10 days after the contract is accepted.

If the report is late, the buyer has a short window to cancel. Personal representatives, trustees and conservators who never occupied the home are excused, which helps heirs selling an estate house in De Pere. Everyone else should answer every item, because a partly filled report is treated as incomplete.

Should you list, or sell your De Pere house for cash?

A listing suits a house that shows well and a seller who can wait on a buyer's financing. A cash sale suits a house with open permits, deferred maintenance, tenants, or a family estate to close.

Whatever the route, ask for a net sheet. It should show the loan payoff, the 30 cents per $100 transfer fee, recording, prorated taxes and any repair credit, so you compare actual proceeds and not asking prices.

At the Brown County Register of Deeds in Green Bay. The office phone is 920-448-4470, and paper submissions need a Swift Agreement under the county's tag-less system.

Only with a Tourist Rooming House license. The city requires a $100 application to Development Services and a pre-inspection by the Health Department sanitarian before any rental.

Buyers can request the city's building records, and open work can come up in negotiation. Starting work without a permit doubles the permit fee, so closing out permits before listing is usually cheaper.

What should a seller in Caledonia, WI know first?

Caledonia is a village in the northeast corner of Racine County, with 25,361 residents at the 2020 census and a Census Bureau estimate of 25,229 on July 1, 2025. Selling a house here means dealing with the village for assessment and permit history, and with Racine County for recording the deed.

Your realistic options are a listing with an agent, a sale by owner, or a direct sale to a cash buyer. Which one fits depends on the condition of the house, whether it sits in the village's older neighborhoods or on a larger rural lot, and how soon you need to close.

How is Caledonia laid out, and why does it matter for a sale?

The village covers about 45 square miles along Lake Michigan, which makes it large by Wisconsin standards. It is made up of distinct communities: Franksville (the old Skunk Grove trading area), Husher, Tabor and others that began as trading posts, railroad stops and crossroads, according to the village's own history page. A buyer looking at a Franksville lot is comparing a different setting from someone looking near Douglas Avenue, and your listing or offer conversation should reflect that.

The village describes easy access to I-94, with Milwaukee 18 miles north and Chicago 73 miles south, plus two business parks (Caledonia and DeBack Farms) that supply local jobs. It also notes the planned Microsoft development in neighboring Mount Pleasant. Commute length matters to buyers, and Census data puts the mean travel time to work for Caledonia residents at 25.8 minutes.

The land has deep roots. An Indian-French fur trader, Jacques Vieau, ran a trading post here around 1832, the Town of Caledonia was created by a territorial act on February 7, 1842, and Bohemian farmers settled in the Tabor area from 1849. The area became a village in January 2006, after a 2005 referendum. For an owner, that history shows up as older farmhouses, long narrow lots near the lakeshore and mixed rural and suburban parcels.

How does the Caledonia assessor affect your sale?

The village has contracted its assessing since 1999 through Cole-Layer-Trumble, now Tyler Technologies. The assessor's job is to place market-based values on all taxable property, and the village states that the assessor does not set tax rates or collect taxes.

  • The village published an assessment ratio of 0.9533 for 2025.
  • The assessor's public hours are Thursdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and clerical staff answer questions Monday through Wednesday mornings.
  • A 2026 preliminary assessment list by address and a 2026 Guide for Property Owners are posted on the assessor page.

The 2026 appeal window has closed. Notices went out July 1, the open-book period ran July 13 to 31, the deadline to give notice of objection was August 17, and the Board of Review met August 19. If you think an assessment is too high before you list, ask the assessor's office when next year's schedule is set. An objection must be filed on form PA-115A at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting, unless the board waives it for good cause.

What permits and building records come up in Caledonia?

The village Building Department issues permits for residential and commercial work, with building, electrical and plumbing inspectors on staff. New homes go through the State of Wisconsin online building permit system, and plumbing and electrical permits are pulled separately from the main application.

For a sale, the practical point is that any work on the house since you bought it should have a closed permit. A buyer's lender or inspector may ask for it, and open work can lower an offer. Call the Building Department with the parcel address and ask for the permit history before you list.

  • A septic mound system needs a sanitary permit from Racine County Planning and Development, so ask that office for records if your lot has one.
  • Rural and lakeshore parcels can have drainage, grading and culvert certifications on file, which the village requires for new homes.
  • Keep copies of final inspection sign-offs with your sale file.

How do you record a deed at the Racine County Register of Deeds?

Caledonia deeds are recorded in Racine County. The county's flat recording fee for a standard document is $30, plus the state transfer fee on the sale. Under Wis. Stat. 77.22 the grantor owes 30 cents per $100 of value, and on a land contract the value is the total principal the buyer agrees to pay.

The Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Return can only be filed online through the Department of Revenue. The Register of Deeds can't help complete it; the county points people to the Department of Revenue at (608) 264-6885 or (608) 266-1594. A deed must also meet the county's checklist:

  • Grantor and grantee are named
  • The grantor's signature is notarized or authenticated
  • A complete legal description is included
  • The parcel identification number is shown
  • The drafter's name and a return address appear on the document
  • The document is legible and follows the state margin rules

The Racine County Register of Deeds phone number is (262) 636-3208. If the owner has died and the deed lists the decedent, ask whether a Termination of Decedent's Property Interest (form HT-110, $30 to record) applies before you sell.

Most sellers must give the buyer a completed real estate condition report within 10 days after the contract is accepted, under Wis. Stat. 709.02. The chapter covers property with one to four dwelling units, and it also covers land with no buildings, which uses a separate vacant land report. That second category matters in a village with rural parcels.

A buyer who does not receive the report on time can rescind within two business days after the 10-day period ends and get any deposit back. Personal representatives, trustees, conservators and court-appointed fiduciaries who never occupied the property are not required to give the report. Everyone else should answer every item, since a report counts as complete only when each item is answered or covered by a permitted substitute.

Is a cash sale or a listing better in Caledonia?

A listing makes sense when the house is current on repairs and you can wait for a buyer's financing. A cash sale makes more sense when the house needs work, has a short payoff clock, or comes with tenants or an estate to settle.

How can you sell a house fast in Mequon, WI?

A buyer who takes the house as it is shortens the list of repairs, showings and negotiations before closing. You can also list with an agent or sell privately, and each route ends with a seller's condition report, a transfer return and a recorded deed.

The Census Bureau reports for Mequon a median owner-occupied home value of $501,600 and an 86.0% owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024. With values at that level, a repair credit or a price cut moves real money, so sellers here weigh an as-is sale against the cost and time of fixing the house.

What is Mequon, Wisconsin like?

Mequon is a city in Ozaukee County about 15 miles north of Milwaukee, on the western shore of Lake Michigan. It covers 48.77 square miles, and as of 2005 it was the third-largest city by land area in the state. Roughly half of the land is undeveloped or farmed, so lots here vary widely in size and in the services that reach them. The Village of Thiensville sits as an enclave in the middle of the city. The city borders Cedarburg and Grafton to the north, Germantown to the west, and Bayside, River Hills, Brown Deer and Milwaukee to the south. Much of the shoreline has mixed gravel and sand beaches, and the soil is clayey glacial till, which is worth knowing if you plan to dig a foundation or a pond.

The Town of Mequon incorporated as a city in 1957 under the state's Oak Creek Law, which was written to keep suburban towns from being annexed. Germans became the largest ethnic group in the 1840s. Growth followed I-43 in the 1960s, and the lakefront runs along clay bluffs that range from 80 to 140 feet high, cut by ravines where streams reach the lake.

Winter highs average about 27 degrees in January and July highs about 81 degrees. The Ozaukee Interurban Trail, a former passenger rail line, runs north to south through the city, and I-43 reaches it through exits 85, 87 and 89.

Does your Mequon house use city sewer and water or a well and septic system?

It depends on the lot, and the city utilities page says some properties receive both services, only water, only sewer, or neither. The sewer utility serves the sanitary sewer service areas that are not using septic or mound systems. The Mequon Water Utility serves Mequon, Thiensville and Bayside, yet quite a few properties still use a private well or a water trust.

This matters at sale time because the state's condition report has a section for wells, septic systems and storage tanks. Before you list, call the Sewer and Water Utilities office and confirm what serves your address.

  • Water: city water from the Mequon Water Utility, or a private well or water trust.
  • Sewer: city sewer in a sanitary sewer service area, or a septic or mound system.
  • Records: gather any septic, well or tank paperwork you hold for the condition report.

The utility reports no lead water mains and no lead service lines, and it has required plastic laterals since service began in 1998. The same page notes that lead can still be found in solder on copper plumbing from before 1986 and in brass faucets and fittings from before 2014.

Which schools and amenities do Mequon buyers look for?

The Mequon-Thiensville School District serves nearly the whole city. Its elementary schools are Donges Bay, Oriole Lane and Wilson, its middle schools are Lake Shore and Steffen, and Homestead High School serves grades 9 through 12. About six square miles in the far northwest are in the Cedarburg School District, so check your address if you live near the Cedarburg line.

Concordia University Wisconsin and a Milwaukee Area Technical College campus are in Mequon, and St. Mary's Hospital Ozaukee opened in 1994. Public transit is limited: the Ozaukee County Express commuter route (Route 143) runs to Milwaukee on weekdays, and a shared-ride taxi covers trips beyond it. Large areas of the city have no sidewalks.

What do city departments handle during a Mequon sale?

Community Development handles zoning, planning and permit forms, and you schedule an inspection by calling (262) 236-2930. Completed permit applications can be returned during office hours, by mail or email, or through the drop box east of City Hall's southern main door.

The Assessor's Office uses methods set by the Wisconsin Property Assessment Manual and Chapter 70 of the Wisconsin Statutes, and all of its staff are certified by the Department of Revenue. The office points owners to City Hall for detailed assessment and property tax information, so ask the city for the current-year assessment before you set a price. The city website also carries pay links for property tax and utility bills.

What does Wisconsin require from a Mequon seller?

The seller pays a real estate transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value under Wis. Stat. 77.22, and at the Mequon median of $501,600 that is about $1,505. The state also requires a condition report for sales of one to four dwelling units, delivered within 10 days after the contract is accepted.

  • A buyer who does not receive the report in time may rescind within 2 business days after the 10-day period and recover deposits.
  • If you learn something before accepting an offer that changes an answer, Wis. Stat. 709.035 calls for an amended report within 10 days of acceptance.
  • Transfers between parent and child for nominal or no consideration and transfers by will or descent are on the Department of Revenue's list of fee exemptions.
  • Understating the value on the return can bring a penalty of $25 or 25% of the additional fee, whichever is greater.

The transfer return is filed electronically on the Department of Revenue site, and you can reach the department's return team at RETR@wisconsin.gov.

How do you record a deed in Ozaukee County?

You record it with the Ozaukee County Register of Deeds at 121 W. Main Street, Room 120, in Port Washington. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and can be reached at 262-284-8260, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 994, Port Washington, WI 53074.

The office also offers a Property Fraud Alert sign-up and a Designation of Transfer on Death form. Recorded transfers become public through the Land Information Office's property transfer report, which lists the transfer fee, parcel number and the grantor and grantee for each document. A sale price can be worked out from that report by dividing the fee by 3 and multiplying by 1,000.

Frequently asked questions

Does every Mequon house have city sewer and water?

No. Some properties have both services, some only water or only sewer, and some neither. Many still use a private well or septic or mound system. Call the Sewer and Water Utilities office to confirm what serves your address.

Which school district serves Mequon?

Mequon-Thiensville School District serves most of the city. About six square miles in the far northwest are served by the Cedarburg School District.

How do I schedule a building inspection in Mequon?

Call Community Development at (262) 236-2930. Permit applications can be returned in person, by mail or email, or through the drop box east of City Hall's southern main door.

How much is the transfer fee on a Mequon house sale?

It is 30 cents per $100 of value, paid by the seller. At the city's median value of $501,600, the fee is about $1,505, collected when the deed is recorded.

Where do I record a deed for a Mequon house?

At the Ozaukee County Register of Deeds, 121 W. Main Street, Room 120, Port Washington. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and answers at 262-284-8260.
